item.title: NASA’s Attempt to Save the Swift Telescope Has Failed
item.description: NASA’s Swift Observatory, which studies some of the most powerful explosions in the universe, will soon burn up in the atmosphere.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: Chinese Start-Up Lands Reusable Rocket for the First Time
item.description: The milestone by the private company, LandSpace, could put China closer to challenging SpaceX’s rule in lower-cost spaceflight.
item.dc:creator: Adeel Hassan

item.title: Moderna, Merck Say mRNA Vaccine Prevents Melanoma From Returning
item.description: Moderna and Merck say the experimental vaccine prevented the return and spread of the cancer in high-risk melanoma patients.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.media:credit: Adam Glanzman/Bloomberg
item.media:description: Cancer vaccine research in the lab at the Moderna Inc. headquarters in Cambridge, Mass.

item.title: Humans Love Having Pets. Seems Like Some Other Primates Do, Too.
item.description: We aren’t the only animals that like to take care of other species. A new study finds that the roots of keeping a pet may stretch deep into our primate past.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mitchell Brown

item.title: How NASA Engineers Are Keeping the Voyagers Alive
item.description: A reworking of the spacecraft’s power systems could extend the nearly 50-year-old Voyagers’ exploration of interstellar space into the early 2030s.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:credit: Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times

item.title: Jaguars Are Ready to Come Back. The Border Wall Might Stop Them.
item.description: A lone male roves the Arizona mountains, and a female has been spotted just across the border in Mexico. The sightings raise hopes for the species, despite serious threats.
item.dc:creator: Douglas Main and Celia Talbot Tobin
item.media:credit: Celia Talbot Tobin for The New York Times
item.media:description: Eamon Harrity, a wildlife program director with Sky Island Alliance, checking a wildlife camera along the border wall in southern Arizona.

item.title: How One Woman With a Very Rare Disease Secured a Clinical Trial
item.description: Through sheer determination, Neena Nizar has become the first patient in a clinical trial testing a treatment for her disease — one so rare it affects just 30 people worldwide.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:credit: Moriah Ratner for The New York Times
item.media:description: Neena Nizar is one of only 30 people worldwide living with Jansen’s disease, a rare disorder that deforms bones. She is Patient No. 1 in a study at the N.I.H. of a drug that might help.

item.title: Telescope Spots Two Black Holes on the Cusp of Merging
item.description: New images from the James Webb telescope show a galaxy with a trio of supermassive black holes. Two of them appear to be locked in a tight tango.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Schupak
item.media:credit: Chris Gunn/NASA
item.media:description: Engineers working with the James Webb Space Telescope’s near-infrared spectrograph. The instrument can tease apart the individual wavelengths of light hitting it, which allowed scientists to observe gases behaving in ways only a black hole’s pull can cause.

item.title: The MOTHRA Telescope Captured the Faint Aftermath of a Star’s Death
item.description: During early calibration tests, the MOTHRA telescope’s array of lenses, which will soon number 1,140, captured stellar debris dissolving into space around the Helix Nebula.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway
item.media:credit: MOTHRA Telescope Array/NASA, ESA, C. R. O’Dell and M. Meixner, P. McCullough and G. Bacon
item.media:description: The Helix Nebula, sometimes called the “Eye of God” because of its eye-like shape, is an example of what a star can look like at the end of its life cycle.

item.title: Former Fauci Adviser Pleads Guilty to Trying to Conceal Covid-Related Records
item.description: Dr. David Morens, a former N.I.H. official, admitted to attempts to conceal emails that discussed the origins of the pandemic.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Mueller
item.media:credit: Annabelle Gordon/Reuters
item.media:description: David Morens, a former National Institutes of Health official, after his arraignment in the U.S. District Court in Greenbelt, Md., in May.

item.title: Trump Nominates Heidi Overton, a Top Domestic Policy Aide, for F.D.A. Commissioner
item.description: Dr. Overton is a fierce opponent of abortion rights and a supporter of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again agenda.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett
item.media:credit: Eric Lee for The New York Times
item.media:description: Dr. Heidi Overton, if confirmed by the Senate, would succeed Dr. Marty Makary, who resigned as commissioner in May.

item.title: Trump Administration Moves to Allow Logging in Pristine National Forests
item.description: The move to repeal the ‘roadless rule’ would pave the way for road construction and logging in nearly 45 million acres of untouched back country.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Friedman and Maxine Joselow
item.media:credit: Ron Niebrugge/Alamy
item.media:description: A bear in the Tongass National Forest of southeast Alaska. Roadless areas make up about 30 percent of all national forest land and are home to more than half of imperiled wildlife, including grizzly bears, wolves, elk, salmon and wolverines.

item.title: Rafting Through the Grand Canyon on a Depleting Colorado River
item.description: As water levels on the Colorado River fall to historic lows, a rafting trip through the canyon feels even more precious.
item.dc:creator: Heather Hansman
item.media:credit: Carl Tremblay/Shutterstock
item.media:description: For rafters beginning their journey on the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon, Navajo Bridge is the last modern structure they see for the trip’s duration.

item.title: Lake Powell Hits Lowest Level On Record As Water Crisis Continues
item.description: Levels in Lakes Mead and Powell have not been so low since 1957, underscoring a water crisis that plagues seven states that rely on the Colorado River.
item.dc:creator: Scott Dance and Mira Rojanasakul
item.media:credit: John Locher/Associated Press
item.media:description: The Glen Canyon Dam near Lake Powell in Arizona last month. Lakes Powell and Mead, the country’s largest reservoirs, have been recording new lows this summer.

item.title: Share Your Experiences With the Public Health System in Louisiana
item.description: The New York Times is examining how public health is changing in the state, from the whooping cough outbreak to vaccine policies, and we want to hear from you.
item.dc:creator: Rosemary Westwood
item.media:credit: Kathleen Flynn/Reuters
item.media:description: A Covid shot being administered at a 2021 drive-through event in Avondale, La.

item.title: How Louisiana’s New Surgeon General Wants to Transform Public Health
item.description: Dr. Evelyn Griffin is pushing for more emphasis on wellness and prevention. She has also aligned with the MAHA movement in fighting government mandates and questioning the safety of some vaccines.
item.dc:creator: Rosemary Westwood
item.media:credit: Christiana Botic for The New York Times
item.media:description: Dr. Evelyn Griffin, Louisiana’s surgeon general, testified in May about a bill that would have prohibited businesses and schools from mandating new vaccines or other medical interventions.

item.title: How Cyclospora Evaded the U.S. Food Safety System to Sicken Thousands
item.description: The Trump administration delayed a rule last year that could have sped up the effort to pinpoint the source of the contamination. Critics charge that food safety oversight has eroded overall.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett and Julie Creswell
item.media:credit: Al Drago for The New York Times
item.media:description: Last year the Food and Drug Administration cut a program that tracked cyclospora outbreaks and delayed a rule that would have required companies to swiftly provide supply chain records in investigations of foodborne disease outbreaks.

item.title: Mining Claims Staked on Land Cut From Bears Ears and Grand Staircase Monuments
item.description: Prospectors are eyeing mineral deposits within the former boundaries of the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monuments in Utah.
item.dc:creator: Maxine Joselow
item.media:credit: George Frey/Getty Images
item.media:description: Both Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monuments are rich in wildlife habitat and archaeological treasures but also sit atop vast reserves of uranium and other precious metals.

item.title: Why Europe Keeps Being Pummeled by Heat Waves
item.description: The whole planet is warming, but changes in weather patterns could help explain why the continent is suffering so many bouts of severe heat.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong
item.media:credit: Fabrice Coffrini/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: A tourist at the parched bed of Lac des Brenets on the France-Switzerland border on Tuesday.

item.title: Judge Rejects Suit Against University of Michigan That Sought Emails on Climate Law
item.description: A conservative group had tried to force the University of Michigan to hand over messages from a law professor who worked on “climate superfund” bills.
item.dc:creator: Karen Zraick
item.media:credit: Peter Hoffman for The New York Times
item.media:description: Rachel Rothschild, a law professor at the University of Michigan, whose emails were being sought in the lawsuit against the school.

item.title: Federal Job Cuts Are Making Wildfires Harder to Fight
item.description: The Trump administration pushed out thousands of veteran U.S. Forest Service staff. An ‘extraordinary’ fire season is testing those who are left.
item.dc:creator: Scott Dance
item.media:credit: Ethan Swope/Associated Press
item.media:description: Firefighters at the Summit fire in Llano, Calif., last month.

item.title: Early-Onset El Niño
item.description: The global weather disrupter appears to be taking a toll, and its peak could still be months away.
item.dc:creator: David Gelles

item.title: This Pesticide May Be Too Dangerous to Use. Farmers Say They Need It.
item.description: California announced that it’s phasing out paraquat, a pesticide widely used in the United States that is linked to Parkinson’s disease.
item.dc:creator: Ted Alcorn
item.media:credit: Bill Barksdale/Design Pics Editorial/Universal Images Group, via Getty Images
item.media:description: American farmers spray millions of pounds of paraquat on crops each year, though experts could not say precisely how much.

item.title: How to Catch the ‘Eclipse of the Century’ in 2027, When Spain, Egypt and More Go Dark
item.description: On Aug. 2, Southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East will witness a solar blockbuster with extra-long totality. If you want to see it, book soon.
item.dc:creator: Danielle Dowling
item.media:credit: Finbarr O'Reilly for The New York Times
item.media:description: The solar eclipse on Wednesday in Castrillo de la Reina, Spain. Next summer’s total solar eclipse will darken a 9,500-mile-long swath from the tip of southern Spain past the Horn of Africa.
